question.:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${11}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${58}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $1$ minute and ${28}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $6$ minutes. The temperature $T(t)$, in degrees Celsius, obeys Newton's law of cooling, with $t$ measured in minutes since cooling began. To the nearest minute, how long after cooling began does the body reach ${16}^{∘}\text{C}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-11),\qquad k>0.
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-11} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-11} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-11| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-11>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-11 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-11 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-11 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =11+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(1)=58$ and $T(6)=28$:

$$
\begin{aligned}58 & =11+Ke^{-1k} \\ 47 & =Ke^{-1k} \\ 28 & =11+Ke^{-6k} \\ 17 & =Ke^{-6k}\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the excess temperatures to eliminate $K$, then take natural logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{47} & =\frac{Ke^{-6k}}{Ke^{-1k}} \\ \frac{17}{47} & =e^{-5k} \\ \ln(\frac{17}{47}) & =-5k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{17}{47} \right)}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(1)=58$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}47 & =Ke^{-1(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{17}{47} \right)}}{5})} \\ K & =47e^{1(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{17}{47} \right)}}{5})} \\ K & =47\left(\frac{47}{17}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=11+47\left(\frac{47}{17}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}}e^{-(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{17}{47} \right)}}{5})t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =11+(47\left(\frac{47}{17}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}})e^{-(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{17}{47} \right)}}{5})\cdot 1}=58 \\ T(6) & =11+(47\left(\frac{47}{17}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}})e^{-(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{17}{47} \right)}}{5})\cdot 6}=28\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the body reaches ${16}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =16 \\ 11+Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =16 \\ Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =5 \\ e^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{5}{K} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\ln\left(\frac{5}{K}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{5}{K}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the values of $K$ and $k$ to obtain the time measured since cooling began:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{17}{47} \right)}}{5}}\ln\left(\frac{5}{47\left(\frac{47}{17}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =1+5\frac{\ln(\frac{5}{47})}{\ln(\frac{17}{47})}≈12\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: T(t)>ambient; positive rate; t>=0; observations strictly cooling
